title: The hidden partner
hookLine: showing off is called a hidden shirk, doing good for people's eyes (Ahmad)

cards: A man stands to pray alone. His prayer is ordinary, a little quick. Then he notices someone has come into the room and is watching.
His back straightens. His recitation slows and grows careful. Every movement becomes more beautiful.
Nothing has changed except the audience. A report in the collection of Ibn Majah uses exactly that picture, and calls it a hidden shirk. Shirk means giving God a partner.
Nobody in that room set up an idol. So where's the partner? Look at who the prayer is suddenly for.

teach.h: RIYA': GOOD DONE FOR PEOPLE'S EYES.
teach.b: Riya'. Showing off: doing good for people's eyes. All week the shahadah has cleared the room.

Riya' is how something slips back in through the side door. First, what the hadith calls it. In the Musnad of Imam Ahmad, the Prophet tells his companions that what he fears for them is the lesser shirk.
They ask what that is. He says: riya'. Not a statue.
An audience. The deed still looks like worship, but part of it is quietly offered to the people watching. Second, the Qur'an names it too.

teach.h: WHO WOULD BE SEEN AT WORSHIP.
teach.b: Surah one hundred seven, in Pickthall's translation, warns of worshippers "Who would be seen (at worship)."
And the end of surah eighteen asks whoever hopes to meet his Lord to "make none sharer of the worship due unto his Lord." Sharer, partner. Third, the tradition's answer is hiddenness.
A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari describes, among those shaded by God on a day with no other shade, a person who gave charity so secretly that his left hand didn't know what his right hand gave.

Fourth, a balance, so this doesn't turn into fear. Sahih Muslim records the Prophet being asked about a man who does good and people praise him for it. He called it the early good news of the believer.

Being seen isn't the problem; doing it to be seen is. And some teachers warn against the opposite trap too: giving up a good deed for fear of what people will think lets the audience run your life all the same.

how: Muslims are taught to check their intention before a good deed, and hadith praise giving charity in secret, while some teachers also warn against abandoning good deeds out of fear of being seen.

o: feeling proud after someone thanks you for a favor
praying in a group instead of praying alone
doing good so that people will see and praise you

games.q: the hidden partner — tap the pairs.
p: who would be seen at worship
left hand doesn't know the right
the early good news of the believer

s: shirk only means bowing to an idol
a hadith calls showing off a lesser, hidden shirk: an audience, not a statue.
being praised for a good deed ruins it
Sahih Muslim calls such praise the early good news of the believer; doing it to be seen is the problem.
the Qur'an warns of worshippers who would be seen at worship

games.q: you're about to do a good deed and you worry someone will see and you'll start doing it for them. what do the teachers say?
o: skip the deed, to be safe.
do it, and keep your intention for God.
do it only when a crowd is watching.
games.why: giving up a good deed because of people is still letting people decide; the remedy is the intention, not the silence.

practice: Let ideas come for one good deed nobody will see: paying for something quietly, fixing what someone else left broken, praying for a person who will never know, a kind word about someone who isn't in the room.
Pick one you could really do, plan it so no one finds out, and notice any small itch to tell; let it pass, like a breath. If you pray, you can make the intention for God alone.

wordCard.voice: Riya'. Showing off: good done for people's eyes, the partner hidden inside a good deed. Today's word.

orig.note: showing off, doing good to be seen; the hadith calls it a lesser, hidden shirk.

carryVoice: Your line: only for him. The left hand doesn't need to know. See you tomorrow.
